mean: to move a planned event to a later time
ex: Ma'am, could we postpone tomorrow's review to Friday? The client's data hasn't reached us yet.
ex2: Because of the heavy rain in Chennai, the school has decided to postpone its annual sports day.
note: The opposite, 'prepone', is Indian English only. In emails abroad, write 'bring forward' or 'move earlier'.

mean: to fix a new time for something that was already planned
ex: The dentist's clinic called to reschedule my Tuesday appointment because the doctor is away at a wedding.
ex2: The airline offered to reschedule our flight to Srinagar at no extra charge because of the snowfall.
note: Postpone = later only; reschedule = any new time, earlier or later. Both ree-SHED-yool and ree-SKED-jool are correct.

mean: easy for you, because it suits your time or plans
ex: Uncle, please let me know a convenient time to come and collect the house papers.
ex2: The new metro station is so convenient that Meera now reaches her Noida office in twenty minutes.
note: Ask 'Is 4 p.m. convenient for you?', not 'Are you convenient at 4?'. The time is convenient, not the person.

mean: to be thankful for something, or to understand its value
ex: I would appreciate it if you could send the rent receipt by the fifth, as my office needs it for HRA.
ex2: We really appreciate the hostel cooks staying back to serve hot dinner after the late match.
note: 'I would appreciate it if you could...' is a polite request. Don't drop 'it': 'I would appreciate if' is a common error.

mean: free to meet or talk; or ready to be used or bought
ex: Are you available for a quick call after lunch? I need ten minutes to go over the invoice.
ex2: Bhaiya, is this blue kurta available in a medium, or only in large?
note: No 'on' before today or tomorrow: 'I'm not available today', not 'on today'. For things: 'Tatkal tickets are available online'.

mean: trouble or difficulty that disturbs your comfort or plans
ex: The society notice read: 'We regret the inconvenience caused by Sunday's water cut in Block C.'
ex2: Indian Railways apologised for the inconvenience after the Rajdhani reached Howrah six hours late.
note: 'Sorry for the inconvenience caused' is correct but overused. Naming the actual problem sounds warmer: 'Sorry the lift was off all morning.'

mean: to ask for something politely or formally
ex: I would like to request two days' leave next week for my sister's engagement in Patna.
ex2: The bride's family made a polite request that guests avoid plastic gift-wrap at the wedding.
note: As a verb, no 'for': 'I request a refund', not 'I request for a refund'. As a noun, 'for' is right: 'a request for leave'.

mean: to check again later on something you asked or discussed earlier
ex: If the bank doesn't reply by Thursday, I'll follow up with the branch manager in person.
ex2: The doctor asked Babuji to follow up in two weeks so she could check his sugar levels again.
note: Verb: two words (follow up). Noun/adjective: hyphen (a follow-up). Also, 'revert' means 'go back', not 'reply'; write 'please reply', not 'kindly revert'.

mean: arriving or doing things at the agreed time, not late
ex: Mr D'Souza is so punctual that the whole staff room could set its clocks by his 8:55 arrival.
ex2: Our milkman is punctual: the doorbell rings at 6:10 every morning, rain or shine.
note: Usually for people or payments. Noun: punctuality. Jokes about 'Indian Stretchable Time' aside, being punctual for interviews and calls is read as respect.

mean: thinking about other people's feelings and needs
ex: It was considerate of our neighbour to warn us before the drilling started for his new kitchen.
ex2: It's considerate to lower your phone's volume in a crowded Delhi metro coach.
note: Don't confuse with 'considerable' (large in amount). Considerate is about kindness; considerable is about size.

mean: to pause before acting because you feel unsure or shy
ex: Please don't hesitate to call me if the plumber doesn't turn up on Saturday.
ex2: At the interview, Nisha did not hesitate when asked why she wanted to leave her old job.
note: 'Please do not hesitate to contact me' is a correct but stiff email ending. 'Feel free to call me' sounds warmer.

mean: done quickly, without delay
ex: Thank you for your prompt reply; the courier reached our Guwahati office the very next day.
ex2: The ambulance's prompt arrival after the crash on the Pune expressway saved the driver's life.
note: Also a verb ('the alarm prompted us to leave'). The adverb 'promptly' means at once or exactly on time: 'promptly at 9'.

mean: polite and respectful in the way you speak and behave
ex: Even when the customer shouted about the late delivery, the call-centre agent in Noida stayed courteous.
ex2: The courteous ticket checker on the Shatabdi helped an elderly couple find their seats and lift their bags.
note: Said KUR-tee-us, not 'kor-shus'. Noun: courtesy ('a courtesy call'). A little more formal than 'polite'.

mean: careful not to share private things or cause embarrassment
ex: Please be discreet about Mohan's surgery; he hasn't told the rest of the team yet.
ex2: The jeweller in Jaipur was discreet and never told anyone how much the family spent on the necklace.
note: Sounds the same as 'discrete' (separate, distinct), but means something different. Noun: discretion ('at your discretion').

mean: not wanting to do something, so slow or unwilling to do it
ex: The landlord was reluctant to return the full deposit, but agreed after seeing photos of the clean flat.
ex2: Six-year-old Aryan was reluctant to share his new cricket bat with his younger cousin.
note: Followed by 'to' + verb: 'reluctant to agree'. 'Hesitant' suggests doubt; 'reluctant' suggests you simply don't want to.

mean: friendly and generous towards guests and visitors
ex: Our hosts in Amritsar were so hospitable that we couldn't leave without a second round of parathas.
ex2: The homestay family in Coorg was hospitable, serving us fresh coffee and akki roti every morning.
note: Both hos-PIT-uh-bul and HOS-pit-uh-bul are correct. Noun: hospitality. An 'inhospitable' place, like a desert, is hard to live in.

mean: kind, polite and generous, even when you don't have to be
ex: Even after losing the final, the Kerala captain was gracious and praised the winners' bowling.
ex2: Our gracious host in Lucknow insisted we take the last kebab, though she hadn't eaten yet herself.
note: 'Gracious in defeat' means losing with dignity. Not the same as 'graceful', which means moving beautifully.

mean: careful to spend little and waste nothing
ex: My frugal grandmother reuses every gift-wrapper and still carries the steel tiffin she bought in 1975.
ex2: As a first-year student in Delhi, Kabir lived a frugal life of Maggi, metro rides and library books.
note: Neutral or positive, unlike 'stingy' or 'kanjoos', which mean unwilling to spend even on others.

mean: to keep delaying something you should do now
ex: I procrastinate on my income tax return every year until the last week of July, then panic.
ex2: Students who procrastinate until the week before the board exams end up memorising instead of understanding.
note: Postponing is a decision to move something; procrastinating is delaying out of habit or avoidance. Noun: procrastination.

mean: willing to accept or agree to a suggestion
ex: If the landlord is amenable, we would like to paint the bedroom ourselves and deduct the cost from the rent.
ex2: The coach was amenable to shifting practice to the evening during Ramzan, so the fasting players could join.
note: Always 'amenable to' + noun or -ing: 'amenable to rescheduling'. Not the same as 'amiable' (friendly) or 'amenities' (facilities).

mean: friendly and polite, but in a slightly formal way
ex: The two families had a cordial meeting over chai and samosas before discussing the wedding dates.
ex2: Even after the boundary-wall dispute, the two neighbours stay cordial and greet each other every morning.
note: Often signals 'polite but not close': 'relations stayed cordial' after a dispute. Indian wedding cards often 'cordially invite' you.

mean: to give or do something in return for what you received
ex: The Rahmans invited us for Eid lunch, so we'd like to reciprocate by hosting them for Onam sadya.
ex2: If a colleague covers your shift during Pongal, reciprocate by covering theirs at Christmas.
note: 'Reciprocate back' repeats itself; the 'back' is already in the word. Noun: reciprocity.

mean: entering someone's private life or space in an unwelcome way
ex: Relatives asking 'When is the good news coming?' at every function can feel intrusive to newly married couples.
ex2: The calculator app asked for access to my contacts and photos, which felt intrusive for such a simple tool.
note: Verb: intrude. 'Sorry to intrude, but...' is a polite way to interrupt someone's private moment or meeting.

mean: to make room for someone, or adjust to meet their needs
ex: The hotel can accommodate your request for a ground-floor room, since your mother uses a wheelchair.
ex2: The small Kolkata flat could accommodate only four guests, so the cousins slept at Mashi's place.
note: Often misspelt in emails: double c AND double m. In British use the noun is uncountable: 'find accommodation', not 'accommodations'.

mean: an embarrassing social mistake, like saying the wrong thing
ex: Asking my aunt her age at the kitty party was a faux pas I will never repeat.
ex2: Wearing shoes into the gurdwara was a faux pas the tourist quickly fixed when a sevadar gently pointed it out.
note: French: the x and s are silent, so say foh PAH. The plural is spelt the same: 'two faux pas'.

mean: perfect, with no mistakes or faults at all
ex: The wedding planner's arrangements in Udaipur were impeccable, right down to the name cards on every table.
ex2: Ramesh's English is impeccable, but at the Kochi fish market he switches to Malayalam to bargain.
note: Usually for manners, timing, taste, service or a record. Stronger than 'very good': it means nothing at all can be faulted.

mean: to help someone remember something they need to do
ex: Can you remind me to pay the electricity bill before the fifteenth?
ex2: Pooja set an alarm on Dadaji's phone to remind him about his evening tablets.
note: Say 'remind me about the meeting' or 'remind me to call', not 'remind me the meeting'.

mean: to say you are sorry for something you did wrong
ex: Rahul called the client to apologise for the late shipment and offered free delivery next time.
ex2: Siddharth's mother made him apologise to the neighbour for breaking the window with his cricket ball.
note: Apologise TO a person FOR a mistake. 'Please accept my apologies' is formal; 'sorry' is everyday.

mean: to plan and prepare something so that it happens
ex: Could you arrange a cab to the airport for our guests from Kolkata?
ex2: Meenu's aunt helped arrange the flowers and diyas on the stage for the school's annual day.
note: Arrange FOR someone to do something: 'I'll arrange for a driver to pick you up.'

mean: to stop yourself from doing something
ex: Guests are requested to refrain from smoking anywhere inside the hotel, including the balconies.
ex2: Nikita tried hard to refrain from checking her phone during the family dinner.
note: Always 'refrain FROM + -ing': 'refrain from talking'. As a noun, a refrain is the repeated line of a song.

mean: to work together, or help willingly when asked
ex: Passengers are requested to cooperate with security staff during baggage checks at the airport.
ex2: If all the flats cooperate and separate their waste, the society can set up its own compost pit.
note: Cooperate = willingly go along and help; collaborate = actively build something together.

mean: to pay back money someone spent for you or for work
ex: The company will reimburse your auto fares for client visits if you submit the receipts by Friday.
ex2: After months of calls, the insurance firm agreed to reimburse Mr Gill for his knee surgery in Ludhiana.
note: You reimburse a PERSON or reimburse the COST. 'Reimburse back' repeats itself; the 're' already means back.

mean: to ask for information about something
ex: I am writing to enquire about the fees for your weekend Kannada classes.
ex2: At the station, Farida went to the counter to enquire whether the Howrah Mail was running late.
note: 'Enquire after someone' means ask how they are. 'Inquire' is often used for official investigations.

mean: happy to help others, even when it means extra trouble
ex: The obliging shopkeeper let us charge our phones while we waited out the downpour.
ex2: Our obliging neighbour in Chandigarh waters our plants every time we go out of town.
note: 'Much obliged' is an old-fashioned thank-you; 'obliging' describes the helpful person.

mean: careful to handle people without upsetting or offending them
ex: When asked whose biryani was better, Dadi gave a diplomatic answer and praised both her daughters-in-law.
ex2: In her email, Maya was diplomatic: she called the client's design 'bold' instead of 'messy'.
note: Close to 'tactful'. It also means relating to embassies, as in a 'diplomatic passport'.

mean: a complaint about something you feel is unfair
ex: Residents can raise any grievance about the water supply at the ward office every Monday.
ex2: Before meeting HR, Lata wrote down her grievance about unpaid overtime so she would not forget anything.
note: Indian offices and colleges often have a 'grievance cell' or 'grievance redressal' system for formal complaints.

mean: by mistake, without meaning to
ex: I inadvertently hit 'Reply All' and sent my leave request to the entire Bengaluru office.
ex2: The bride's uncle inadvertently locked the car keys inside, delaying the baraat by half an hour.
note: Useful in polite apologies: 'I inadvertently left your name off the list' sounds better than 'I forgot'.

mean: to make a process happen faster
ex: Could you please expedite my refund? It has been three weeks since I returned the phone.
ex2: The hospital helped expedite the visa papers so the patient's family could fly in from Dhaka.
note: Formal and common in office emails. Soften it with 'could you please', since you are asking someone to hurry.

mean: deserving praise
ex: Anita's effort to run a free tuition class in her village while doing her MSc is truly commendable.
ex2: The ground staff did a commendable job, drying the Eden Gardens outfield in time for the evening match.
note: Formal and warm; ideal for reviews, speeches and thank-you notes. A notch below 'outstanding'.

mean: quiet and not drawing attention, so it does not disturb anyone
ex: The waiters at the reception were unobtrusive, refilling glasses without interrupting a single conversation.
ex2: The new CCTV cameras in the library are small and unobtrusive, tucked above the bookshelves.
note: The opposite of 'intrusive'. A compliment for service, design and good house guests.

mean: a cheerful, friendly feeling among people
ex: The bonhomie at the office Holi party made even the strict finance head laugh.
ex2: There was easy bonhomie between the two captains at the toss, despite the fierce rivalry.
note: French for 'good-natured'. Indian newspapers love it for photo-ops. Say BON-uh-mee, not 'bon-HO-mee'.

mean: very careful to follow rules, manners and small details correctly
ex: Our punctilious landlord notes every nail hole in the walls before returning the deposit.
ex2: The punctilious host at the Lucknow dinner made sure every guest was served before he took a bite.
note: Not the same as 'punctual' (on time). Punctilious is about details and correct behaviour.
